# Worksheet: When Predictors Tell the Same Story

[📥 Grassland data](data/grassland_c3.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="grassland_c3.csv"} [📥 Tools script (.R)](themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R){.btn .btn-primary download="r_themes_and_functions.R"} [📥 Script skeleton (.R)](11_multiple_regression_homework.R){.btn .btn-primary download="11_multiple_regression_homework.R"}

**The study.** Paruelo & Lauenroth surveyed **73 grassland sites** across central North America and recorded what fraction of the plant community was **C3 grasses** — the cool-season photosynthetic type. For each site they recorded six climate and geography variables that might explain it.

**The question.** What controls the abundance of C3 grasses?

**How this relates to class.** In class the Loyn bird data had mild collinearity: grazing lost significance once patch area was in the model, but nothing reversed. These data are worse. Two of these predictors carry almost the same information, and which of them you include decides not just the size of a slope but its **sign**.

Columns: `c3_proportion`, `mean_annual_precip_mm`, `mean_annual_temp_c`, `summer_precip_prop`, `winter_precip_prop`, `longitude`, `latitude`.

::: callout-note
**Before you start**

There is no hidden "right" model to find. You are graded on whether your conclusion follows from your diagnostics — and on whether you can say plainly what these data cannot resolve.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 1 · Setup and the data

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(car)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

grass_df <- read_csv("data/grassland_c3.csv") %>%
  mutate(log_c3 = log10(c3_proportion + 0.1))

grass_df
```

> 💡 The response is logged because `c3_proportion` is a bounded proportion with zeros in it. The `+ 0.1` keeps `log10()` from returning `-Inf`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 2 · One predictor at a time

**▶ Run this** — fit each predictor on its own, exactly as in class:

``` r
# ── Part 2.1 · One predictor at a time ──────────────────────────────────
lm(log_c3 ~ mean_annual_temp_c, data = grass_df) %>% summary()

lm(log_c3 ~ latitude, data = grass_df) %>% summary()
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Record both, then say what each one claims on its own.

```
mean_annual_temp_c: slope = __________  p = __________

latitude:           slope = __________  p = __________

In words: ___________________________________________________
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 3 · Put them in the same model

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 3.1 · Put them in the same model ───────────────────────────────
temp_lat <- lm(log_c3 ~ mean_annual_temp_c + latitude, data = grass_df)

summary(temp_lat)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Compare the temperature slope with what you got in Part 2.

```
Temperature slope alone     = __________  p = __________

Temperature slope with lat  = __________  p = __________

What happened to the sign? __________________________________
```

# Part 4 · Diagnose it

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · Diagnose it ──────────────────────────────────────────────
grass_df %>%
  select(mean_annual_precip_mm, mean_annual_temp_c, summer_precip_prop,
         winter_precip_prop, longitude, latitude) %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)

vif(temp_lat)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Find the two most strongly correlated predictors in the matrix.

```
Strongest pair: __________ and __________   r = __________

VIF for temperature and latitude: __________ and __________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** The VIFs are nowhere near the "VIF > 10 is bad" rule of thumb, yet the slope still flipped sign. What does that tell you about rules of thumb?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 5 · The full model

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · The full model ───────────────────────────────────────────
full_model <- lm(log_c3 ~ mean_annual_precip_mm + mean_annual_temp_c +
                   summer_precip_prop + winter_precip_prop +
                   longitude + latitude,
                 data = grass_df)

summary(full_model)

vif(full_model)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Six predictors go in. How many come out significant, and which?

```
Significant: ________________________________________________

Overall model p = __________   R squared = __________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** The overall F-test is highly significant while five of six predictors are not. Explain how both can be true at once.

```
____________________________________________________________

____________________________________________________________
```

# Review and checkpoint

At this point you can:

- [ ] Fit and interpret a multiple regression with several continuous predictors
- [ ] Recognise a sign reversal as a symptom of collinearity rather than a new finding
- [ ] Use a correlation matrix and VIFs, and explain why the VIF rule of thumb is not a safety net
- [ ] Explain a significant overall F alongside non-significant individual predictors
- [ ] Compare models on adjusted R² and AIC and defend a choice
- [ ] State plainly what a dataset cannot resolve
